periods.label: First decade
periods.coverage_label: Volumes 1–10, through 10(2); available sample: volumes 8–9 and 10(1–2)

categories.name: Defence expenditure studies
categories.note: Expenditure research is split between spending/growth, demand and strategic interactions, and national budget-policy topics. The first-period Greek expenditure model sits in spending/growth, so these are overlapping scope correspondences rather than exclusive classifications.
categories.definition: Demand for military expenditure, its economic consequences and the behaviour of spending over time.

categories.name: Procurement processes and policies
categories.note: Procurement and industrial cooperation now form a distinct topic. Equipment costs form another, with no assignments in this early sample. The reviewed government repair-contract model is assigned to strategic models; procurement incentives are therefore still split across topics.
categories.definition: How defence equipment is purchased and how procurement arrangements and incentives operate.

categories.name: Economics of alliances
categories.note: Alliance public goods, burden sharing and contribution incentives are recognisable. The reviewed NATO peacekeeping and international-status studies also show that this topic is broader than any single alliance activity.
categories.definition: Alliance provision and contributions, including burden sharing and public goods; later retrospectives also include common European defence cooperation.

categories.name: Conversion
categories.note: The Kaliningrad conversion paper is assigned to the wider industries/firms/innovation topic. Conversion is represented within that topic but is not a separate cluster.
categories.definition: The adjustment of military resources and industries towards civilian uses.

categories.name: Defence industries and industrial base
categories.note: Industry structure and innovation sit in one topic; procurement-driven industrial policy and cooperation sit in another. The Dutch industry interface and Spanish procurement examples illustrate the overlap.
categories.definition: The structure, organisation and performance of defence producers and their industrial base.

categories.name: Military manpower
categories.note: Recruitment, retention, service and military labour form a recognisable pooled topic, but it has no assigned abstracts in the available first-period sample.
categories.definition: Military labour supply, recruitment, retention and the organisation of service personnel.

categories.name: Country surveys
categories.note: Country surveys remain a publication format rather than a separate substantive cluster. The reviewed Turkey survey is assigned to spending/growth; surveys cannot be counted by using that entire topic.
categories.definition: Country-focused surveys of defence economics; a survey format rather than a single substantive topic.

categories.name: Terrorism, guerrilla warfare, and insurgencies
categories.note: The combined category spans the separate terrorism, civil-conflict and strategic-model topics. The early sample has no terrorism assignments; its civil-conflict example concerns democracy and peace, while its strategic-model example concerns contracting. These counts do not establish first-decade insurgency prevalence.
categories.definition: Economic analysis of terrorism and armed insurgency, combined in the original first-decade grouping.

categories.name: Defence and growth
categories.note: Growth is prominent in the spending/growth topic, including the reviewed Turkey country survey, but the early topic also contains a Greek expenditure-demand model. Its count is not an exclusive growth-paper total.
categories.definition: The relationship between defence expenditure and economic growth.

categories.name: Public choice and defence
categories.note: Political institutions and distributional questions form a separate pooled topic, while incentive and principal-agent models can occur in the strategic topic. No political-economy abstracts are assigned in this early sample; the strategic example is government contracting, not a standalone public-choice category.
categories.definition: Political decision making, incentives and collective choice applied to defence.

categories.name: Regional economics and defence
categories.note: Regional economics is not independently resolved. The Kaliningrad conversion example occurs within the industry topic; that entire topic cannot be treated as regional research.
categories.definition: Regional and local economic dimensions of defence activity and expenditure.

categories.name: Defence R&D, technological change, and weapon development
categories.note: Innovation, industrial procurement and equipment capability/cost research overlap the R&D category across three topics. None is an exclusive R&D cluster, and equipment-cost assignments are absent from the available early sample.
categories.definition: Research, technological progress and the development of military equipment.

categories.name: Military posture and strategic policy
categories.note: National defence budgets and policy now form a recognisable topic. The reviewed French policy and force-structure papers support this overlap, but the cluster extends beyond military posture alone.
categories.definition: The economic dimensions of strategic choices and the configuration of military forces.

categories.name: Arms races
categories.note: The weapons/arms topic includes the reviewed increasing-returns arms-race model; the expenditure-interaction topic includes the Greek-Turkish arms-race study. The two clusters also contain work outside arms racing.
categories.definition: Strategic interaction and competitive accumulation of armaments.

categories.name: Arms trade
categories.note: The arms topic combines trade, production, arms races and weapons strategy. The reviewed production-in-less-industrialised-countries paper illustrates its wider scope. The original first retrospective reports five arms-trade papers, whereas the later summary reports six.
categories.definition: International transfers of weapons and the economics of arms markets.

categories.name: Disarmament and arms control
categories.note: The increasing-returns arms-race paper explicitly discusses arms-control agreements, but arms control is not independently resolved from the wider weapons/arms topic.
categories.definition: The economics of reducing and limiting armaments.

categories.name: Others
categories.note: The residual editorial category is not a coherent thematic seed or a single model cluster. Unassigned model abstracts are a different concept and are not equated with Others.
categories.definition: Residual papers outside the named categories; not a single research theme.

categories.name: Military production function
categories.note: Firm productivity/efficiency and equipment cost-effectiveness provide related scope, but neither cluster is an exclusive military input-output production-function category.
categories.definition: The relationship between military inputs, outputs and productive efficiency.

categories.name: Nature of defence economics
categories.note: Seeding the conceptual-foundations theme did not produce an independently resolved foundations/history cluster. Similarity-based seed matches are not used as editorial labels.
categories.definition: The scope and conceptual foundations of defence economics as a field.

categories.name: Defence budgets
categories.note: The national budget-policy topic includes budgeting, force structure and strategic choices. It is a wider topic than budget formulation and allocation alone.
categories.definition: The formulation and allocation of defence budgets.

categories.name: Developing countries and defence
categories.note: The reviewed Turkey spending/growth survey illustrates a developing-economy application within a wider macroeconomic topic. That topic is not an exclusive developing-country classification.
categories.definition: Defence economics questions focused on developing economies.

periods.label: Second decade

categories.name: Defence and the economy
categories.note: The most direct correspondence is the defence-spending/growth topic. The editorial category covers wider macroeconomic effects, while debt and political/distributional effects appear in separate topics. This is not a complete count of economic-impact studies.
categories.definition: The broad economic impact and effects of defence expenditure, including growth and other macroeconomic outcomes.

categories.name: Terrorism
categories.note: Terrorist behaviour, its determinants and counterterrorism form a recognisable theme. Some financial-market consequences occur in the risk/markets topic; close scope does not establish article-level agreement.
categories.definition: Economic analysis of terrorist behaviour, its consequences and counterterrorism.

categories.name: Defence policies, planning and management
categories.note: This broad editorial grouping is split across procurement/industrial cooperation, equipment costs/replacement, and national budgets/policy. Each whole-topic count also includes content beyond the editorial category.
categories.definition: A broad policy grouping including procurement, budgeting and allocation, military policy and posture.

categories.name: Conflict and civil wars
categories.note: Conflict is now split between civil-conflict/war/peace research and strategic contest/intervention models. The former also includes peacekeeping and other conflict research; the latter includes broader game-theoretic models. Their scopes are not identical to the editorial category.
categories.definition: The economics of conflict and civil war, including their causes and consequences.

categories.name: Defence industries and industrial base
categories.note: Firms, industrial performance and innovation form one topic, while industrial procurement/cooperation forms another. These topics also overlap R&D and policy; neither count is an exclusive industrial-base total.
categories.definition: The structure, organisation and performance of defence producers and their industrial base.

categories.name: Peace and peacekeeping
categories.note: Peacekeeping financing and post-conflict peace overlap civil-conflict research, strategic intervention and collective-contribution models. Personnel and country-policy studies also contain peacekeeping applications. There is no standalone peacekeeping cluster, so these whole-topic series cannot verify the editorial decline.
categories.definition: Economic analysis of peace and activities that maintain peace.

categories.name: Arms races, arms control and disarmament
categories.note: Arms competition/control overlaps the mixed weapons/arms topic and expenditure-interaction research. Trade, production and other spending-demand studies are also present; neither topic is an exclusive arms-control category.
categories.definition: Arms competition together with policies and agreements to constrain or reduce armaments.

categories.name: Economics of alliances
categories.note: Alliance public goods, contributions and burden sharing remain recognisable, including NATO and historical alliances. The topic also includes some collective peacekeeping-finance research, while industrial cooperation can occur in the procurement topic.
categories.definition: Alliance provision and contributions, including burden sharing and public goods; later retrospectives also include common European defence cooperation.

categories.name: Defence R&D and technology
categories.note: The reviewed procurement-driven technological-change, collaborative-development and capability/cost studies illustrate research distributed across industry/innovation, procurement/cooperation and equipment-cost topics. The model has no exclusive R&D cluster.
categories.definition: Research and development and technological change in the defence sector.

categories.name: Fiscal effects of defence spending
categories.note: The debt topic isolates a narrower public-finance theme, with reviewed military-spending/external-debt studies. Other budgetary and fiscal consequences are not captured by its count alone.
categories.definition: Public-finance consequences of military spending, rather than all macroeconomic effects.

categories.name: Military personnel and recruitment
categories.note: Recruitment, retention, military service, training and labour-market outcomes are recognisable. The topic also contains some peacekeeping and other labour applications, so the scopes are not identical.
categories.definition: Military labour, recruitment, retention and personnel issues.

categories.name: Models of defence expenditures
categories.note: Demand and strategic expenditure interactions form a distinct topic, but national budget-policy models and political-regime determinants also occupy separate topics. The reviewed Greece-Turkey, national-policy and regime studies illustrate the split.
categories.definition: Modelling and explaining the determination and patterns of defence expenditure.

categories.name: Arms trade
categories.note: Trade is embedded in a wider weapons/arms topic that also includes arms racing, intelligence and production. Its whole-topic count must not be read as an arms-trade-paper total.
categories.definition: International transfers of weapons and the economics of arms markets.

categories.name: Country surveys
categories.note: Country surveys remain dispersed by substantive content. The reviewed Canadian and Norwegian policy surveys illustrate national-policy assignments; other surveys occur in spending, industry or alliance topics. There is no survey-format cluster.
categories.definition: Country-focused surveys of defence economics; a survey format rather than a single substantive topic.

categories.name: Others
categories.note: The residual editorial category is not a coherent thematic seed or a single model cluster. Unassigned model abstracts are a different concept and are not equated with Others.
categories.definition: Residual papers outside the named categories; not a single research theme.

categories.name: Regional economics and defence
categories.note: Regional studies are not independently resolved. The reviewed south-west England supply-chain and spatial-growth studies occur in broader industry or spending/growth topics, whose full counts cannot represent regional research.
categories.definition: Regional and local economic dimensions of defence activity and expenditure.

method.basis: Fifteen fixed topics from the published pooled, retrospective-guided model, counted by publication volume and issue; no per-decade refits.
method.training: The published BERTopic model was guided by 20 seed themes consolidated from the names and definitions in these same three retrospectives. Additional model themes were allowed; not all seeds became separate topics.
method.independence: Correspondence is partly by design because the retrospectives supplied the seeds. This comparison is not independent validation of the model or a measure of classification accuracy.
method.model_denominator: All abstract-bearing records in the matching period, including unassigned abstracts.
method.editorial_denominator: The classified-paper total in each original retrospective, excluding separately listed book reviews.
method.crosswalk: Curated after reading period-specific representative abstracts and targeted scope examples. Mappings describe selected, overlapping scopes, not exclusive editorial assignments; topic counts repeat across rows and must not be added.
method.limits: Editorial categories, fifteen guided model clusters and available abstracts are different classifications and populations. Seed similarity scores do not define this crosswalk. Similar counts are not accuracy estimates, and an unresolved seed does not establish that a research theme was absent.
method.review: Two nearest original members to each period-specific final-topic centroid, falling back to final members where needed, were read in full; additional peacekeeping, sanctions, piracy and company-survey abstracts were checked. All distances used original document embeddings.
